Category theory
Category theory basics for JavaScript developers: types as objects, functions as morphisms, and the composition laws of identity and associativity.
Understand what a category is in programming, with types as objects and functions as morphisms, and which two laws their composition obeys.

There is a close connection between functional programming and category theory. In functional programming many abstractions, laws and principles are taken from category theory.
So what do we know about category theory? We will not dive into the fundamentals and academic terms. We will try to explain all of this without academic terminology.

A category, in the context of programming, is a collection of objects (data types: Array, Object, Number, String, ...) and morphisms between them (arrows, that is, functions). Morphisms f :: a -> b and g :: b -> c can be composed into g . f :: a -> c (read as "g after f": first f, then g). Composition obeys two laws. Identity: every object has an identity morphism id :: a -> a, and composing with it changes nothing (f . id = f, id . f = f). Associativity: h . (g . f) = (h . g) . f, so it does not matter where the parentheses go.
